title: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder: A Case Report
case_prompt:
A 38-year-old patient presented with progressive bilateral visual loss over four months, accompanied by throbbing temporal headache. There was no eye redness, vomiting, or neck stiffness. On ophthalmologic examination, the patient could count fingers at three meters, and fundoscopic examination showed pale optic discs bilaterally, consistent with optic atrophy. Brain MRI was normal. Topical betaxolol was administered without visual improvement.

One month later, the patient was evaluated by neurology for persistent headache and bilateral visual loss of five months' duration. Repeat fundoscopic examination confirmed bilateral optic atrophy. There was no memory deficit, other cranial nerve palsies, sensory or motor deficits, or bladder/bowel dysfunction. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed normal chemistry and cellularity, and repeat brain MRI remained normal. A diagnosis of idiopathic intracranial hypertension was made; the patient was treated with acetazolamide and serial lumbar punctures, reporting slight visual improvement.

Three months later, the patient was admitted with one week of lower-extremity weakness, numbness, and tingling, along with bladder and bowel dysfunction. Vision had deteriorated further during this period. On examination, blood pressure was 100/60 mmHg, pulse 90/min, respirations 24/min, and temperature 37.2°C. The patient was alert and oriented. Visual acuity was counting fingers at two meters. There was flaccid paraplegia and sensory loss below the T4 dermatome. No meningeal signs were present.

Laboratory studies showed normal complete blood count, liver and renal function, and urinalysis. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis B and C, and VDRL were negative. CSF protein was elevated at 145 mg/dL; glucose was 55 mg/dL; no cells or organisms were seen; CSF VDRL was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. T2-weighted spine MRI demonstrated a long, central T3–T6 hyperintense lesion with mild cord expansion and proximal central canal dilation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Multiple sclerosis less likely — “Patchy, peripheral, short spinal segment lesions are a common finding in multiple sclerosis.”  
2. Opticospinal lupus excluded — “The lack of other clinical features of SLE and negative serological test for ANA exclude opticospinal lupus.”  
3. Neurosarcoidosis unlikely — “Normal chest X-ray finding does not favor sarcoidosis.”  
4. Subacute combined neurodegeneration improbable — “Absence of risk factors for vitamin B12 deficiency like malabsorption of any cause makes SCND less likely.”  
5. Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder supported — patient has optic neuritis and acute myelitis with a longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis lesion in the absence of AQP4-IgG testing.
